deepDiveThesesUsed.summary: Apps advertise '60+ supported models' but the vendored llama.cpp build only recognizes specific LLM_ARCH_* tags, so many trending releases (e.g. Qwen3.x) silently can't load.

The GGUF quant label (e.g. Q4_K_M) is not a standardized artifact — different quantizers (and even a vendor's own official QAT release) produce measurably different quality/size under the identical nominal tag.

The app's July 10 Swift rewrite fixed the July 7 staleness gap by fetching llama.cpp's latest GitHub release at build time instead of a pinned old commit, but that fetch resolves 'latest' fresh every build with no pinned tag and no version ever surfaced to the user, so two builds cut hours or days apart can silently embed different sets of supported architectures with no way to tell which one shipped. Backed by real llama.cpp release-cadence data (3 tags in under 3 hours) and PR merge-time data (~1 day to 24 days depending on whether an architecture is genuinely new). Adjacent to but distinct from the 07-07 thesis: static staleness vs. dynamic non-determinism.

PrismML's Bonsai 27B (1.125 bits/weight, 3.9GB, 89.5% of FP16 quality) and reports that Apple is in acquisition/licensing talks with the 3-person Caltech team that built it, undercut the assumption that Apple's own Foundation Models team leads on-device compression. Distinct from the prior GGUF-quant-label and engine-architecture theses: this is about an MLX-vs-GGUF ecosystem/format split (native low-bit training vs. post-hoc quantization), not an LLM_ARCH_* tag gap, and about an external vendor's compression technique rather than our own engine's version pinning.

Nvidia's July 15 Jetson Thor T2000/T3000 launch (16GB/32GB, vs the 2025 flagship T5000's 128GB) deliberately cuts memory to dodge an 80-90% QoQ DRAM price spike (Counterpoint Research) driven by HBM/datacenter AI eating DRAM fab capacity (Micron: cloud-related DRAM revenue 17%->50%, 2023-2025). Independently verified this is not just an edge-silicon story: IDC/TrendForce/Omdia/Counterpoint smartphone-market data (Feb-Jul 2026) shows the identical squeeze already hitting phones -- 12.9% shipment decline forecast, ASP up 14% to $523, sub-$400 phones -22%, memory now ~60% of BOM for sub-$400 phones, RAM price stabilization not expected before mid-2027. Distinct from all four prior deep-dive theses (engine arch gating, quant-label variance, engine version pinning, Bonsai/MLX format split): this is about hardware memory economics and on-device AI's implicit 'RAM only grows' roadmap assumption, not engine/format tooling.

A public Apple Silicon LLM benchmark (john-rocky/apple-silicon-llm-bench) shows llama.cpp costs 0.25 J/token generating Gemma 4 E2B on iPhone 17 Pro vs 0.11 J/token for Apple's own Foundation Models path (a different, smaller system model, not a fair apples-to-apples fight) — and that a naive CoreML/ANE port of the SAME open model is actually worse per-token (0.48 J) than either GPU path despite drawing less than half the power, disproving 'just target the ANE, it's automatically efficient'. Distinct from the prior four theses: this is about runtime energy physics under sustained real-world use, not model compatibility, quant labeling, or hardware memory economics.

Xiaomi's shipping VLA (predecessor to the newly announced Xiaomi-Robotics-1) is 4.7B params and runs in 80ms on one RTX 4090 — smaller than several models already in privateSLM's own catalog and far smaller than its headline-grabbing successor, for reasons rooted in real-time control latency rather than cost-cutting. User-directed piece, distinct from the DRAM/memory-economics and Apple-moat theses.

Liquid AI's July 21 technical report (arXiv:2607.15232) on LFM2.5-8B-A1B's in-place tokenizer expansion (65K->128K vocab) puts a real, vendor-published number on a mechanism none of the prior seven theses touch: on-device decoding is memory-bandwidth-bound at batch size 1, so a larger vocabulary's LM-head matrix costs every user 7-10% slower per-token decode, permanently, in exchange for up to 4x fewer tokens (Thai) for previously under-served languages. Distinct from engine-arch compatibility, quant-label variance, engine-version pinning, MLX/GGUF format fragmentation, DRAM economics, ANE runtime energy, and VLA-latency theses: this is about tokenizer/vocabulary architecture as a silent, per-language on-device performance tax that no benchmark leaderboard discloses.

llama.cpp release b10089 (2026-07-22 19:45 UTC, PR #25962 by @pwilkin) closed a gap where CUDA's GET_ROWS op couldn't handle k-quantized/i-quantized/mxfp4 embedding tables, silently falling back to a full CPU round-trip on every token — while CPU, Metal, Vulkan and SYCL already had complete type coverage. Fixing it took Qwen3-1.7B decode from 6.18 to 1.72 ms/token (3.6x) on the author's own benchmark. Distinct from all eight prior theses: this is a runtime data-movement bug inside one backend's compute graph, not a compatibility/labeling/format/economics/energy story, and it's the first thesis about an engine bug that specifically penalizes small models harder than large ones (the CPU-copy overhead is roughly fixed per token, so it's a bigger fraction of a small model's total decode time).

The Flutter app (and its vendored llama.cpp source used for the old ENGINE COMPATIBILITY gate at packages/maid_llm/src/llama_cpp) now lives only on branch flutter-legacy / tag v2.2.0-flutter, frozen since 2024-08-09. docs/weekly-slm-routine.md (this automation's own spec) was not updated for the pivot and still points at file paths that no longer exist on main.

CRITICAL GAP: the new native engine is NOT version-pinned. scripts/fetch-llama.sh always downloads whatever is the LATEST ggml-org/llama.cpp GitHub release at build time — no tag/commit is recorded anywhere in the repo, the resulting Frameworks/llama.xcframework is gitignored (not committed), there is no CI that would capture which version went into any given build, and no App Store release/tag exists yet for the native app (README still self-describes as 'Phase 0 — engine spike', which is itself stale given Phases 1-4 already merged). This means there is currently NO reliable, checkable source of truth for which GGUF architectures the shipping engine supports — the ENGINE COMPATIBILITY hard gate (quality bar #5) cannot be verified against a stable reference. Until fetch-llama.sh is pinned to an explicit tag/commit (recorded in-repo) or a real App Store release ships with recorded engine version, catalog-compatibility checks in this routine are working from the OLD flutter-legacy llm_arch enum as the conservative fallback, since it's the only fixed, inspectable reference and it's plausible some live installs are still running that build.

TOOLING NOTE for future runs: pushing binary images via the GitHub MCP create_or_update_file tool by reading a base64-encoded file into context is extremely token-expensive (a 58KB JPEG becomes ~78KB of base64 text, tens of thousands of tokens, and gets truncated by the Read tool's pagination on long single-line files). Direct 'git clone' of the two configured repos over the session's local git proxy (already credentialed, confirmed working: git clone https://github.com/mega-studios/privateslm-site.git succeeds without any extra auth setup) works fine and lets images, HTML, and JSON all be written and committed locally with zero base64-in-context cost, then pushed with a normal 'git push'. Used that approach for this run's image commits; recommend it as the default for any future run that needs to commit binary assets.
